# Introduction

Supplement to the paper "Confidence intervals for the F1-score in medical object
detection: comparing bootstrap and Bayesian multilevel methods".

This script evaluates the simulation study: coverage, bias and width of the 95% intervals
of recall, precision and F1-score. The simulation itself (data generation, model fits,
bootstrap, extraction of the data files) is in the folder `simulation/` of the repository.

Code and data: <https://github.com/ndevln/f1-score-ci-object-detection> (data:
`S3_Data_ML_Estimates.csv.xz`, `S3_Data_Pathologist_Estimates.csv.xz`,
`S3_Data_Objects_per_Image.csv`).

**ML design** (one rater per image, as the ML models of the examples): 4 image scenarios x
2 image counts (40, 100) x 500 replicates with 4 (A-C) or 3 (D) performance variants
= 15,000 datasets.

- Scenarios (objects P per image): D very low (P = 1 + Poisson(0.5), median 1, mean 1.5),
  A low (median 4, 43% of the images with P <= 3), B broad (median 20), C bimodal (median 22,
  20% large images).
- Variants of A-C: 1 base (recall 0.8, 2 FP per image + 0.05 FP per object, image SDs
  0.8 / 1.2, correlation 0.7); 2 FP independent of P; 3 higher performance (recall 0.9, 1 FP
  per image); 4 low image heterogeneity and lower performance (recall 0.65, 3.1 FP per image,
  image SDs 0.3 / 0.4).
- Variants of D (fewer FP, as in radiology; image SDs 0.8 / 1.2, correlation 0.7, no FP per
  object): 5 baseline (recall 0.8, 0.1 FP per median image, about 0.2 FP per image on
  average); 6 more FP (0.5 FP per median image, about 1.0 on average); 7 conservative operating
  point (recall 0.65, 0.05 FP per median image, about 0.1 on average).
- Methods: image bootstrap (pooled and grouped); Bayesian binomial + Poisson model; Bayesian
  multinomial model as a comparison model (both models defined in the Appendix); Wilson interval
  of the pooled recall and precision (objects treated as independent, no F1).

**Pathologist design** (every pathologist scores every image, as in Example 1): 3 image
scenarios (A-C) x 2 variants x 100 replicates = 600 datasets with 40 images.

- Variants: 1 "data example" (23 pathologists, mainly differing in their cutoff),
  2 "skilled panel" (9 pathologists, mainly differing in skill).
- Average pathologist (the population of pathologists): row bootstrap (image x
  pathologist rows), cluster bootstrap (images with all pathologists), two-way bootstrap
  (images and pathologists); Bayesian binomial + Poisson model with new pathologists and with
  the observed pathologists (as in Example 1).
- Single pathologist (one new pathologist, prediction interval): stratified bootstrap
  (images within each pathologist), cluster bootstrap; Bayesian binomial + Poisson model.

**Estimands and truths:** marginal pooled and grouped values of the superpopulation of
images (and of the population of pathologists), computed from expected counts. The estimates of
the average of the *observed* pathologists (Example 1: cluster bootstrap and the Bayesian model
with the observed pathologists) are compared with the population of pathologists as well, to show
that they do not generalize to other pathologists.

**Evaluation:** 95% quantile intervals (QI); point estimate = median of the bootstrap or
posterior draws (Wilson: observed proportion and Wilson score interval). Coverage = share of the datasets whose interval contains the truth; for the
single pathologist the mean share of the 20,000 per-pathologist truths inside the interval.
Monte Carlo SE of the coverage = sd / $\sqrt{n}$ over the $n$ datasets of a table cell
(for a share of 95% about 0.2 pp with 12,000 datasets, 0.5 pp with 2,000, 1.0 pp with 500 and
2.2 pp with 100). The cells (scenario x image count) are ordered by the expected number of
objects per dataset (mean P x number of images), e.g. "D 40 (60)".

# Setup
## Load Packages
```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Functions
`summarise_coverage()` summarises grouped datasets: coverage, its Monte Carlo SE, bias and
width. `format_coverage()` prints the coverage as "93.6 (0.2)" (Monte Carlo SE in brackets)
and rounds the other columns.
```{r}
summarise_coverage <- function(df) {
  df |>
    summarise(
      datasets = n(),
      coverage = 100 * mean(covered),
      mc_se    = 100 * sd(covered) / sqrt(n()),
      bias     = mean(bias),
      width    = mean(width),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

format_coverage <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      coverage = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", coverage, mc_se),
      across(c(bias, width), \(x) round(x, 3))
    ) |>
    select(-mc_se, -datasets)
}
```

## Objects per Dataset
Expected number of objects per dataset: mean P of the superpopulation of a scenario times the
number of images. It orders the cells and the scenarios (D, A, B, C) from few to many objects.
```{r}
read_csv("S3_Data_Objects_per_Image.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  cross_join(tibble(n_slide = c(40, 100))) |>
  mutate(objects = round(mean_P * n_slide), mean_P = round(mean_P, 2)) |>
  arrange(objects) |>
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%s %d (%s)", scenario, n_slide,
                        format(objects, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)),
         cell = factor(cell, levels = cell)) -> df_cells

df_cells
```

# ML design
## Load Data
Estimates of all methods (95% QI and Wilson intervals), joined with the truths.
```{r}
scenario_levels <- df_cells |> distinct(scenario, mean_P) |> arrange(mean_P) |> pull(scenario)

df_ml <- read_csv("S3_Data_ML_Estimates.csv.xz",
                  show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  left_join(df_cells |> select(scenario, n_slide, objects, cell), by = c("scenario", "n_slide")) |>
  mutate(
    scenario  = factor(scenario, levels = scenario_levels),
    scenarios = if_else(scenario == "D", "D (variants 5-7)", "A-C (variants 1-4)"),
    method = factor(method_id,
                    levels = c("bootstrap", "binomial_poisson", "multinomial",
                               "wilson"),
                    labels = c("Bootstrap (images resampled)", "Bayesian binomial + Poisson",
                               "Bayesian multinomial", "Wilson binomial CI")),
    # Short names for the tables
    method_short = factor(method, labels = c("Bootstrap", "Bayes B+P", "Bayes multinomial",
                                             "Wilson")),
    covered = as.numeric(.lower <= truth & truth <= .upper),
    bias    = value - truth,
    width   = .upper - .lower
  )
```

## Coverage, bias and width
Coverage, bias and width of the intervals per metric, scenario and image count, ordered by the
expected number of objects per dataset (all variants; A-C: 2,000, D: 1,500 datasets per point;
Monte Carlo SE of the coverage about 0.5 pp near 95%, up to 1.2 pp where the coverage drops).
Long format for the facets: one row per measure (coverage, bias, width).
```{r}
measure_levels <- c("Coverage (%)", "Bias", "Width")

df_ml |>
  group_by(name, averaging, method, cell) |>
  summarise_coverage() |>
  pivot_longer(c(coverage, bias, width), names_to = "measure") |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = c("coverage", "bias", "width"),
                          labels = measure_levels)) -> df_ml_cells

# Reference lines: 95% coverage, zero bias
tibble(measure = factor(measure_levels[1:2], levels = measure_levels),
       value = c(95, 0)) -> df_reference

# Axis limits: coverage up to 100%, bias at least -0.02 to 0.02 (tiny biases do not look large)
tibble(measure = factor(measure_levels[c(1, 2, 2)], levels = measure_levels),
       value = c(100, -0.02, 0.02)) -> df_limits
```

Figure template without data and facets; one figure per metric is the template plus the data of
the metric (`plot + df` replaces the plot data) and the facets with the metric in the row labels
(e.g. "F1-score CI coverage (%)"), kept in a named list (Supplement Figures S3.1-S3.3; Figure 4 of the paper).
```{r}
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = cell, y = value, color = method, group = method)) +
  geom_hline(data = df_reference, aes(yintercept = value), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_blank(data = df_limits, aes(y = value), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  # Wilson in vermillion (6th Okabe-Ito colour)
  ggokabeito::scale_color_okabe_ito(name = NULL, order = c(1, 2, 3, 6),
                                    guide = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 90)) +
  labs(x = "Scenario, number of images (expected number of objects per dataset)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.placement = "outside") -> ggplot_template_ml

# Named list (F1, Precision, Recall)
df_ml_cells |>
  split(~name) |>
  imap(\(df, metric) {
    metric_label <- if_else(metric == "F1", "F1-score", metric)
    ggplot_template_ml + df +
      facet_grid(measure ~ averaging, scales = "free_y", switch = "y",
                 labeller = labeller(measure = \(x) case_match(
                   x,
                   "Coverage (%)" ~ paste(metric_label, "CI\ncoverage (%)"),
                   "Bias"         ~ paste0(metric_label, "\nbias"),   # bias of the point estimate
                   "Width"        ~ paste(metric_label, "CI\nwidth")
                 )))
  }) -> plots_ml_cells
```

Dashed: 95% coverage and zero bias. Figure 4 of the paper shows the same without the multinomial model."

### Supplement Figures S3.2 and S3.3

Precision and recall: the same, with the Wilson interval for the pooled estimand. The Wilson
interval treats all objects as independent; its width shrinks with the number of objects,
while the uncertainty depends on the number of images.
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Supplement Figure S3.2: Coverage, bias and mean width of the 95% intervals of the precision in the ML design, as in Supplement Figure S3.1; Wilson interval for the pooled estimand only."
#| fig-height: 6.5
plots_ml_cells$Precision
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Supplement Figure S3.3: Coverage, bias and mean width of the 95% intervals of the recall in the ML design, as in Supplement Figure S3.1; Wilson interval for the pooled estimand only."

plots_ml_cells$Recall
```

## Overview
Coverage in % (Monte Carlo SE), mean bias and width: scenarios A-C (12,000 datasets) and D (3,000 datasets).
```{r}
df_ml |>
  group_by(scenarios, name, averaging, method = method_short) |>
  summarise_coverage() |>
  format_coverage()
```

Bootstrap: bootstrap with images resampled; Bayes B+P: Bayesian binomial + Poisson model; Bayes
multinomial: Bayesian multinomial model; Wilson: Wilson binomial CI (pooled recall and precision).

## F1-score per variant
Coverage in %: variants v1-v4 of scenarios A-C (3,000 datasets each), v5-v7 of scenario D
(1,000 datasets each).
```{r}
df_ml |>
  filter(name == "F1") |>
  group_by(averaging, method = method_short, variant) |>
  summarise_coverage() |>
  mutate(variant = paste0("v", variant),
         coverage = sprintf("%.1f", coverage)) |>
  select(averaging, method, variant, coverage) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variant, values_from = coverage)
```

Bootstrap: bootstrap with images resampled; Bayes B+P: Bayesian binomial + Poisson model; Bayes
multinomial: Bayesian multinomial model.

# Pathologist design
## Load Data
Estimates of all methods (95% QI), joined with the truths. For the single pathologist the share of
the per-pathologist truths inside the interval replaces the comparison with one truth.
```{r}
df_path <- read_csv("S3_Data_Pathologist_Estimates.csv.xz",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    method = factor(method_id,
                    levels = c("bootstrap_row", "bootstrap_stratified", "bootstrap_cluster",
                               "bootstrap_two_way", "binomial_poisson",
                               "binomial_poisson_observed"),
                    labels = c("Row bootstrap", "Stratified bootstrap", "Cluster bootstrap",
                               "Two-way bootstrap",
                               "Bayesian binomial + Poisson (new pathologists)",
                               "Bayesian binomial + Poisson (observed pathologists)")),
    # Short names for the tables
    method_short = factor(method, labels = c("Row bootstrap", "Stratified bootstrap",
                                             "Cluster bootstrap", "Two-way bootstrap",
                                             "Bayes B+P (new)", "Bayes B+P (obs.)")),
    single  = estimand == "single_pathologist",
    covered = if_else(single, share_inside, as.numeric(.lower <= truth & truth <= .upper)),
    bias    = value - truth,   # NA for the single pathologist (no single truth)
    width   = .upper - .lower
  )
```

## Average pathologist
Coverage of the population value of the pathologists in % (Monte Carlo SE), mean bias and
width, 300 datasets per variant.
```{r}
df_path |>
  filter(!single) |>
  group_by(name, averaging, variant, method = method_short) |>
  summarise_coverage() |>
  format_coverage()
```

Bayes B+P (new): Bayesian binomial + Poisson model with new pathologists; Bayes B+P (obs.): with
the observed pathologists (as in Example 1).

## Single pathologist
Mean share (%) of the 20,000 per-pathologist truths inside the interval (Monte Carlo SE) and
the mean width, 300 datasets per variant.
```{r}
df_path |>
  filter(single) |>
  group_by(name, averaging, variant, method = method_short) |>
  summarise_coverage() |>
  format_coverage() |>
  select(-bias)
```

Bayes B+P (new): Bayesian binomial + Poisson model with one new pathologist.

# Appendix: Bayesian models {.unnumbered}

## Binomial + Poisson model {.unnumbered}
The main model is the model of the paper (Eq. 6-12). For image $i$ and subject $j$:
$$TP_{ij} \sim \text{Binomial}(n = P_i,\ p = recall_{ij}), \qquad FP_{ij} \sim \text{Poisson}(FPR_{ij})$$
$$\text{logit}(recall_{ij}) = \alpha_{recall} + u_{i,recall} + v_{j,recall}, \qquad
\log(FPR_{ij}) = \alpha_{FPR} + u_{i,FPR} + v_{j,FPR}$$
with image random effects $u_{i,recall} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{image,recall})$ and
$u_{i,FPR} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{image,FPR})$, and correlated subject random effects
$(v_{j,recall}, v_{j,FPR}) \sim MVN(0, \Sigma_{person})$.

- ML design: one subject (the ML model) per dataset, so the model has no subject effects $v_j$.
- Pathologist design: the full model with the pathologists as subjects.
- Expected counts of image $i$: $TP_i = recall_{ij} \cdot P_i$, $FP_i = FPR_{ij}$.

## Multinomial model {.unnumbered}
Comparison model of the ML design. The counts of image $i$ are one multinomial outcome with TP as
reference category:
$$(TP_i, FN_i, FP_i) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(N_i = TP_i + FN_i + FP_i,\
(\pi_{i,TP}, \pi_{i,FN}, \pi_{i,FP})\right)$$
$$\log\frac{\pi_{i,FN}}{\pi_{i,TP}} = \alpha_{FN} + u_{i,FN}, \qquad
\log\frac{\pi_{i,FP}}{\pi_{i,TP}} = \alpha_{FP} + \beta \, \widetilde{\log P_i} + u_{i,FP}$$
with $\widetilde{\log P_i}$ the log number of objects centred on the mean of the dataset and
image random effects $u_{i,FN} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{image,FN})$ and
$u_{i,FP} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{image,FP})$.

- Recall and precision of image $i$: $recall_i = \pi_{i,TP} / (\pi_{i,TP} + \pi_{i,FN})$,
  $precision_i = \pi_{i,TP} / (\pi_{i,TP} + \pi_{i,FP})$.
- Expected counts of image $i$: $TP_i = recall_i \cdot P_i$,
  $FP_i = TP_i \cdot \pi_{i,FP} / \pi_{i,TP}$.

## Priors, sampling and estimates {.unnumbered}

- Priors: brms defaults, except the intercept of the FP part of the binomial + Poisson model:
  student_t(3, 1, 2.5) on $\alpha_{FPR}$. The prior was fixed for the simulations, since the 
  brms default is centred on the log median FP count of the data. Because the models were compiled 
  once and refitted on every dataset, a data-dependent prior would be the one of the compile dataset.

| Parameter | Binomial + Poisson | Multinomial |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\alpha_{recall}$ | student_t(3, 0, 2.5) | - |
| $\alpha_{FPR}$ | student_t(3, 1, 2.5) (fixed) | - |
| $\alpha_{FN}$, $\alpha_{FP}$ | - | student_t(3, 0, 2.5) |
| $\beta$ | - | flat |
| $\sigma_{image,\cdot}$ | half-student_t(3, 0, 2.5) | half-student_t(3, 0, 2.5) |
| $\sigma_{recall}$, $\sigma_{FPR}$ (pathologist design) | half-student_t(3, 0, 2.5) | - |
| $\rho$ (pathologist design) | LKJ(1) | - |

- Sampling: brms with cmdstanr, 4 chains with 4,000 iterations each, 1,000 warm-up, thinning 3
  (4,000 posterior draws).
- Marginal pooled and grouped estimates as in the paper: per posterior draw the expected counts of
  the observed images, averaged with Bayesian bootstrap weights over the images (pooled: weighted
  sums of the counts, grouped: weighted mean of the per-image metrics); point estimate = median,
  95% quantile interval.
- Pathologist design:
  - average observed pathologist (as in Example 1): their fitted subject random effects
  - average pathologist: the population of pathologists, 200 new pathologists
    from the subject random effects per draw
  - single pathologist: one new pathologist per draw
  - the Bayesian bootstrap weights are shared by all pathologists of an image
